# Trips: from port to port {#sec-trip}

::: {.callout-note}
**Drafted by AI, in part.** "The sources, best first" was written by Claude (Anthropic) on 2026-10-20. It uses ramb's
example data, and, where those hold no declared trips or landings, one Icelandic trawler's 2019 (background, figures
only). The other sections are still a skeleton, outlined from the maintainer's direction (plan 033 §4) and the
reading map of the groups' reports (`ices_reports.yml`). Reviewed by: nobody yet.
:::

```{r setup}
#| include: false
invisible(Sys.setlocale("LC_CTYPE", "en_US.UTF-8"))
library(tidyverse)
library(duckdbfs)
library(ramb)
library(patchwork)
source("../R/paths.R")
theme_set(theme_minimal())

## ramb's Danish tracks and harbours, flagged as in the previous chapter --------------------------------------
dansk <- rb_read_example("dansk") |> collect() |>
  rename(vid = vessel_id, time = time_stamp) |> arrange(vid, time)
harbours <- rb_read_example("dansk_harbours") |> collect()
harbours <- sf::st_sf(port_id = harbours$SI_HARB,
                      geometry = sf::st_as_sfc(structure(harbours$geometry, class = "WKB"), crs = 4326))
pings <- dansk |> rb_flag_ping_invalid() |> rb_flag_ping_impossible(method = "clean") |>
  filter(is.na(ping_flag)) |> rb_flag_ping_port(harbours)

## One Icelandic trawler's 2019, as fishycode builds it (background) ------------------------------------------
TRAWLER <- 1277
lb_trips <- open_dataset(fd_curated("logbook", "trip.parquet")) |>
  filter(vid == TRAWLER, year(T1) == 2019, is.na(twin) | twin != "duplicate") |>
  select(.tid, schema, T1, T2) |> collect()
ais_voyages <- open_dataset(fd_curated("ais", "voyage.parquet")) |>
  filter(vid == TRAWLER, year == 2019) |> collect()
trip_voyage <- open_dataset(fd_curated("link", "trip_voyage.parquet")) |>
  filter(vid == TRAWLER, year == 2019) |> select(.tid, schema, voyage_id, T2_ais) |> collect()
landings <- open_dataset(fd_curated("landing", "landings.parquet")) |>
  filter(vid == TRAWLER, year(date) == 2019) |> select(.lid, date) |> collect()
trip_landing <- open_dataset(fd_curated("logbook", "lid_map.parquet")) |>
  filter(schema == "afli") |> collect() |> semi_join(lb_trips, by = c(".tid", "schema"))
```

**In the diagram:** row 1, *Trip* (`assign_trip`). Its sources, best first: the declared trip (logbook) → the landing
(`T2`, and `T1` if given) → the voyage from port calls on the track → gaps and the device's power. The band below it:
**link and reconcile**, since trips, landings and voyages are linked many-to-many.

## The problem

- A trip groups pings and records: everything a vessel did between leaving port and returning.
- Declared dates are not arrival times. The logbook's return can be written in advance, and the landing's date is
  when the fish were sold. Only the track measures the arrival.
- Many small boats have no port list, no logbook, and some no tracker that runs in port.

## What the groups say

- A fishing trip runs from leaving port to arriving in port with fishing in between, and several trips can fall on
  one day (WKSSFGEO 2022, p. 13).
- Trips from harbour polygons in the Danish data (WKSSFGEO 2022, p. 9); anchoring sites for small-scale fleets
  (WGSFD 2025a, p. 45).
- Trips cut at gaps (WGSFD 2025a, p. 32); trip ends from the device's power (WKSSFGEO2 2023, pp. 20-21).
- Cleaning logbook trips (WGSFD 2025a, pp. 14-15); trips without pings kept apart (WGSFD 2025a, p. 24); merging tracks
  with logbooks and sales notes (WGSFD 2025a, p. 50); the low match of tracks to sales notes (WKSSFGEO2 2023, p. 4).
- Linking logbook and VMS by vessel and date (WGSFD 2013, pp. 13-14).

## From ramb's articles

- *trips* ("Step 1: cut the track into voyages", "Putting the trip back on the pings"): `rb_create_voyages()` and
  `rb_create_port_calls()` on `dansk`, with the methods compared; `rb_add_voyages()` back onto the pings.
- *trips* ("The cut, in maps"): interactive maps of the cut, one layer per trip. These can stay interactive, since
  the data are public.
  - "Two clean trips": `EX_3`, September 2020, two voyages out of port 917.
  - "When the rules disagree": `EX_10`, July 2014, out of port 141. The runs rule cuts seven voyages that year and
    jepol five, and the difference is one afternoon.
- *trips* (closing note): `rb_add_logbook_trip()` builds the VMS-to-logbook crosswalk.

## The sources, best first

A trip is everything a vessel did between leaving port and coming back. The best source for it is a declared trip in
a logbook, with its departure and return. Next come the landing (its date and port) and the vessel's own track, cut
into voyages at its port calls. Last come the silences in the track, where no port list exists. The cases below use
ramb's example data where those hold the source, and one Icelandic trawler where they do not: no ramb set carries a
logbook trip or a landing. The trawler is the one from @sec-at-sea, followed through 2019.

### Declared trip: the logbook

The logbook declares when the trip started and ended. Many logbooks, the Icelandic one among them, give only the
dates. The trawler's May 2019 shows what that means (@fig-trip-may). The track says the first trip ended with the
vessel in port at 09:54 on 5 May. The logbook gives 6 May, the day the catch was landed. Where one trip ends and the
next begins on the same day, the dates alone cannot say which pings belong to which.

```{r}
#| label: fig-trip-may
#| fig-cap: "One Icelandic trawler, May 2019: its voyages from the track (exact times), its logbook trips (dates only) and its landings (dates). The track measures the arrival; the declarations give the day, often the landing day."
#| fig-height: 2.6
rows <- c("voyage (track)", "logbook trip", "landing")
bars <- bind_rows(
  ais_voyages |> transmute(row = rows[1], from = T1, to = T2),
  lb_trips |> transmute(row = rows[2], from = T1, to = T2)
) |> filter(from >= as.POSIXct("2019-05-01", tz = "UTC"), from < as.POSIXct("2019-06-01", tz = "UTC")) |>
  arrange(row, from) |>
  group_by(row) |> mutate(shade = if_else(row_number() %% 2 == 1, "a", "b")) |> ungroup() |>
  mutate(row = factor(row, rev(rows)), fill = paste(row, shade))
dots <- landings |> filter(month(date) == 5) |> transmute(row = factor(rows[3], rev(rows)), at = as.POSIXct(date) + hours(12))
ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = bars, aes(x = from, xend = to, y = row, yend = row, colour = fill), linewidth = 5) +
  geom_point(data = dots, aes(at, row), size = 3, colour = "#4F81BD") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("voyage (track) a" = "grey20", "voyage (track) b" = "grey55",
                                 "logbook trip a" = "#E69F00", "logbook trip b" = "#F5C26B"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_datetime(date_breaks = "3 days", date_labels = "%d %b") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

Over the whole year (@fig-trip-dates, left), the logbook's return date is the arrival day for most trips, the next
day for some, and a few days off for a handful. A declared date is a day, and the wrong day often enough that it
cannot place the arrival.

### Landing: the sales note

The landing is recorded by the buyer or the authority, not the skipper, and carries the date the catch was weighed or
sold. For the trawler, every 2019 trip has exactly one landing. Most fall on the day the track brings it into port,
some on the day after, and a few further off (@fig-trip-dates, right). A landing can also cover several trips, as a
weekly sales note does in many small-scale fisheries. This trawler has none, and that case is added with simulated
data.

```{r}
#| label: fig-trip-dates
#| fig-cap: "The trawler's 2019: how many days after the track's arrival the logbook gives the return (left) and the landing is dated (right)."
#| fig-height: 2.8
arrive <- trip_voyage |> transmute(.tid, schema, arrived = as_date(T2_ais))
d_lb <- lb_trips |> inner_join(arrive, by = c(".tid", "schema")) |>
  transmute(days = as.numeric(as_date(T2) - arrived), what = "logbook return")
d_la <- trip_landing |> inner_join(arrive, by = c(".tid", "schema")) |>
  transmute(days = as.numeric(date_land - arrived), what = "landing date")
bind_rows(d_lb, d_la) |>
  mutate(what = factor(what, c("logbook return", "landing date"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(days)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~ what) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = -5:5) +
  labs(x = "days after the track's arrival", y = "trips")
```

### Voyage: from port calls on the track

The track needs no declaration. Wherever the vessel stays in port long enough, that is a port call, and a voyage runs
from one port call to the next. ramb finds the port calls with `rb_create_port_calls()` and cuts the voyages with
`rb_create_voyages()`. Here a port call needs four hours in port, the rule ramb's flow uses (`method = "dwell"`). One
Danish vessel's September 2020 has five port calls and six voyages (@fig-voyage-map, @fig-voyage-time). A short stop
in port, under four hours, does not end a voyage.

```{r}
#| label: fig-voyage-map
#| fig-cap: "One Danish vessel (`dansk`, EX_3), September 2020: its voyages cut at port calls of four hours or more, each in its own colour, with the harbour polygon."
#| fig-height: 4.5
ex <- pings |> filter(vid == "EX_3", time >= as.POSIXct("2020-09-01", tz = "UTC"),
                      time < as.POSIXct("2020-10-01", tz = "UTC"))
calls <- rb_create_port_calls(ex, ports = harbours, method = "dwell", min_dwell_h = 4)
voyages <- rb_create_voyages(ex, port_calls = calls, method = "dwell")
ex_v <- ex |> rb_add_voyages(voyages, port_calls = calls)
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = harbours |> filter(port_id %in% calls$port_id), fill = "#E69F00", alpha = 0.4, colour = NA) +
  geom_path(data = ex_v |> filter(!is.na(trip_id)) |> arrange(trip_id, time),
            aes(lon, lat, colour = factor(trip_id), group = trip_id),
            linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2", name = "voyage") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-voyage-time
#| fig-cap: "The same month on a time axis: speed from the track, the port calls (orange) and the voyages between them (grey)."
#| fig-height: 3
g1 <- ggplot(ex, aes(time, speed, colour = !is.na(port_id))) +
  geom_point(size = 0.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#E69F00", `FALSE` = "grey50"), labels = c("at sea", "in port"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "speed (kn)")
g2 <- ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = calls, aes(x = T_in, xend = T_out, y = "port call", yend = "port call"),
               colour = "#E69F00", linewidth = 4) +
  geom_segment(data = voyages, aes(x = T1, xend = T2, y = "voyage", yend = "voyage"),
               colour = "grey30", linewidth = 4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
g1 / g2 + plot_layout(heights = c(2, 1))
```

### Gaps and device power

Many small boats have no port list, and some trackers stop reporting in port. Then the trip can only be read from the
silences: a gap longer than some hours ends one trip and starts the next (WGSFD 2025a, p. 32). ramb's Irish inshore
VMS (`wkssfgeo2_irl_gillnets`) is such a set: four gillnetters, a ping every ten minutes at sea, and long silences
between trips.
The provider marks 136 trips. A silence of two to four hours cuts the track into exactly those 136 trips. A shorter
threshold splits trips at short gaps at sea, and a longer one merges trips that follow each other closely
(@fig-gap-rule).

```{r}
#| label: fig-gap-rule
#| fig-cap: "Trips from silences alone, Irish inshore VMS (`wkssfgeo2_irl_gillnets`). Left: the number of trips a gap rule finds at each threshold, against the provider's 136 (dashed). Right: one vessel's first months, each provider trip in its own colour, with the gaps over four hours marked."
#| fig-height: 3.4
irl <- rb_read_example("wkssfgeo2_irl_gillnets") |> collect() |> mutate(vid = as.character(vid)) |> arrange(vid, time)
cut_at <- function(x, h) x |> group_by(vid) |>
  mutate(gap = as.numeric(difftime(time, lag(time), units = "hours")), seg = cumsum(is.na(gap) | gap > h)) |> ungroup()
found <- map_dfr(c(1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 24), function(h) tibble(hours = h, trips = nrow(distinct(cut_at(irl, h), vid, seg))))
n_provider <- nrow(distinct(irl, vid, trip))
h1 <- ggplot(found, aes(hours, trips)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = n_provider, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 24)) +
  labs(x = "silence that ends a trip (hours)", y = "trips found")
one <- irl |> filter(vid == first(vid)) |> filter(time < min(time) + days(60)) |> cut_at(4)
h2 <- ggplot(one, aes(time, lat, colour = factor(trip))) +
  geom_point(size = 0.3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_vline(data = one |> filter(gap > 4), aes(xintercept = time), colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "latitude")
h1 + h2 + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1.6))
```

Not every trip finder treats a silence as an end. CNR-IRBIM's finder (`method = "cnr"`) joins two voyages across a
silence unless the silence starts and ends inside a coastal zone it is given. Without that zone, as here, it joins
the Irish trips into a handful of long ones. That is a design choice for trackers that drop out at sea, not a fault,
and the comparison of methods below returns to it. A tracker that logs its own power marks trip ends directly, when
it is switched off and on (WKSSFGEO2 2023, pp. 20-21). Such a log is held outside ramb for now.

### The band: link and reconcile

Logbook trips, landings and voyages are linked to each other, not chosen between. One logbook trip can match two
voyages, two trips can share one voyage, and a voyage can carry no trip at all. Over 2019 the trawler's 61 logbook
trips each match one voyage, and two voyages carry two trips each (@tbl-links). Six voyages carry none. Four are
short moves of under two hours, one of them between two neighbouring ports, and the other two are a passage to
Reykjavík and back. A voyage is any movement; a trip is a fishing trip.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-links
#| tbl-cap: "The trawler's 2019: how its logbook trips, voyages and landings link up."
tibble(
  link = c("logbook trips", "voyages", "voyages with one logbook trip", "voyages with two logbook trips",
           "voyages with no logbook trip", "landings", "logbook trips with one landing"),
  n = c(nrow(lb_trips), nrow(ais_voyages), sum(table(trip_voyage$voyage_id) == 1),
        sum(table(trip_voyage$voyage_id) == 2), sum(!ais_voyages$voyage_id %in% trip_voyage$voyage_id),
        nrow(landings), sum(table(trip_landing$.tid) == 1))
) |> knitr::kable()
```

The reconciled trip takes its departure and arrival from the track and keeps the declarations linked to it. That
table is an output of this row, never fed back to redo the declarations' own match: the dates that linked them are
the very dates the track corrects.

## Methods compared

- One track, five trip finders: `dwell`, `runs`, `jepol` (DTU), `cnr` (CNR-IRBIM) and `iapesca` (Ifremer). Data:
  `dansk` and `dansk_harbours`; the published trips `wkssfgeo_cnr_dansk_trips` and `wkssfgeo_cnr_dansk_ping_trips`
  as a check. Start from the trips article's `EX_10` afternoon, where runs and jepol part ways.
  - Graphic: the trips of each method as rows of bars on one time axis, and a table of agreement.
- Port polygons against learned mooring sites. Data: `wkssfgeo_adriatic_passive` and `wkssfgeo_cnr_med_harbours`.

## What if a source is missing

- No port list: trips from gaps and stops only. Show how many trips merge or split against the full answer.
- No logbook: voyages only, with no declared trips to reconcile.
- Sparse pings: port calls missed when the tracker is silent in port. Show this by thinning `dansk`.

## Checking it

- Labelled trips in the workshops' sets (`wkssfgeo_pt_gps`, `wkssfgeo2_irl_pots`): the share of trips matched within
  ±10 % of their duration.

## In the ICES data call

- The data call takes trips from the logbook and ties pings to them by time. It is a clean design where logbooks
  are complete, and this chapter shows what it misses where they are not.

## With ramb

- `rb_create_port_calls()`, `rb_create_voyages()`, `rb_add_voyages()`, `rb_link_trip_voyages()`,
  `rb_link_trip_landings()`, `rb_link_trip_logbook()`, `rb_detect_crosses_year()`.

## Not yet in ramb

- Mooring sites learned from the track; the
  Irish gap rule and the power-on rule as methods.
